title: the later book — Sita's second exile, Lava and Kusha, Sita's return to the earth

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kusha and Lava, named for a handful of grass, singing their father's story before him without knowing it. Did you hear a family story in full? Today, the last time Sita stands before Rama. Day six hundred sixty-six.

Sita's name means furrow. Back in the first book, King Janaka was plowing a field for a ritual when the plow turned up a baby girl in the earth. He raised her as his daughter and named her for the furrow she was found in. Hold on to that, because the Ramayana remembers it. Today the girl from the furrow, now the mother of two grown boys, is brought before a great assembly and asked, one more time, to prove herself.
screen: `SITA MEANS FURROW.` → `FOUND IN A PLOWED FIELD.` → `ASKED ONCE MORE TO PROVE HERSELF.`

segments.voice: When Rama learns that the singing boys are his sons, he sends word to Valmiki. If Sita is pure, he says, let her come and swear it here, before everyone, so the people can see. The next morning the assembly fills: sages, kings, ordinary people from every corner. Valmiki walks in first, and Sita follows behind him, head bowed, hands folded. Valmiki speaks for her. He tells Rama that these are his sons, and that Sita is blameless, and he stakes on it all the merit of his long life of austerity. Rama answers that he believes it, and that he sent her away because of what people were saying. But the oath is still asked of her. Then Sita speaks. She makes three solemn declarations, each built the same way. If I have never thought of anyone but Rama, let the earth goddess open and give me a place. If I have honored him in mind, word and deed, let the earth receive me. As she finishes, the ground splits. A shining throne rises from below, held up by serpents, and the earth goddess herself takes Sita in her arms and seats her there. The throne sinks back down, and the earth closes. The assembly cries out. Rama is wild with grief, and angry at the earth itself. The girl found in a furrow has gone home to the ground she came from. And the poem does not tell us what to feel about it.
screen: `LET HER SWEAR IT BEFORE EVERYONE.` · `VALMIKI SPEAKS FOR HER.` · `IF I HAVE NEVER THOUGHT OF ANOTHER.` · `THE EARTH OPENS AND TAKES HER HOME.` · then, large: `THE GIRL FROM THE FURROW GOES HOME.`

segments.voice: If you can, sit on the floor, or put your bare feet flat on the ground. Feel the weight of your body handed down into the earth. You don't have to hold yourself up right now; the ground is doing it. With each out-breath, let a little more weight go down. Stay with the steadiness underneath you. The bell holds the time.
Sita. Her name means furrow, the field where she was found, and the earth she returns to after her oath before the assembly.
Your line: the earth opens. Today, notice one time someone is asked to prove themselves again and again, and wonder, quietly, what that costs them. Day six hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Sita's return to the earth is told in Hindu homes, songs and stage plays, often with deep grief for her; devotees honor Sita as a goddess in her own right, linked with the earth and with Lakshmi.

pairs: takes her onto a rising throne

myth: Sita was found in a plowed field
Janaka turned her up with the plow, and named her for the furrow.
Sita refuses to speak at the assembly
she makes solemn declarations: if she has never thought of another, let the earth receive her.
Rama is calm when the earth takes her
the text shows him overwhelmed with grief, even angry at the earth.

fork.setup: you're Sita, before the whole assembly, asked once more to prove yourself. what do you do?
options: swear the oath and go home with Rama.
refuse and walk back to the hermitage.
call on the earth to receive you.
fork.reveal: she declares her faithfulness and asks the earth to open. it does, and the earth goddess takes her.

original.note: Sanskrit sītā: the furrow a plow makes. Sita was found in one, and goes back into the earth.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sita proves her innocence and the story ends happily.
what it means: she makes her oath, and the earth opens and takes her; Rama is left grieving.
what a scholar hears: Sita's name, the furrow, links her birth from the earth in the Bala Kanda to her return to it in the Uttara Kanda.
